Caption: Supplementary Fig. 1 | Fleet composition and annual inventory. a, Model-eligible registry records by vessel type. LL, PS, TP and SA denote longline, purse seine, transport and auxiliary vessels. These are registry counts rather than annual active-fleet estimates. b, Sum of annual fleet-group emission medians by vessel type, including historical reconstruction and tuna-share allocation.
Supplementary Table 1 | Data interfaces and quality checks

Supplementary Fig. 2 | PMM donor diagnostics. a, Empirical cumulative distributions of positive observed tonnage and power and the five retained PMM donor candidates. Axes use GT and kW on log scales. The imputed fleet has a different composition, so marginal distribution differences are not a calibration failure by themselves. b, Retained imputed records as a fraction of the registry used in the inventory. Donors describe uncertainty in missing engineering values; observed values are not imputed.
Supplementary Table 2 | Imputation and allocation rules

Supplementary Fig. 3 | Historical missing-capacity reconstruction. a, Required historical power gaps and reconstructed capacity, summed across eligible flag–gear groups. The near-overlap reflects the capacity-closing rule, not independent validation of the historical target. b, Prescribed gradual reduction factor, constant through 1995 and zero from 2017. Alternative gradual-reduction periods are not shown because their legacy outputs were not rebuilt with the repaired data.
Supplementary Table 3 | Engineering conversions and operating assumptions

Supplementary Fig. 4 | Historical data coverage and reconstruction balance. a, Recorded catch on rows with and without positive allocated GHG. b, Fraction of summed fleet-group annual median emissions assigned to spatial records. Observations end in 2024; the 2025 zero reflects missing spatial records. c, Required historical gaps and reconstructed historical power. Catch without allocated GHG remains a coverage gap, rather than a zero-emission observation.

Supplementary Fig. 5 | Accounting identity and technology-correction sensitivity. a, CEI log slopes versus the sum of the two factor slopes on identical years. Agreement checks algebra and implementation only. b, Emission-weighted nominal and technology-adjusted factor trends on identical saved grid samples and fixed weights, separately by gear and era. Hollow symbols denote unadjusted effort and filled symbols corrected effort; arrows show the deterministic correction shift. CEI is invariant while component signs can change. No alternative biological fits are implied.
Supplementary Table 4 | Production stock estimates and sampling diagnostics

Supplementary Fig. 6 | All retained JABBA CPUE series. Observed technology-corrected indices and fitted medians for the 25 retained gear–organisation series. Ribbons show the fitted 95% intervals; they are not independent prediction intervals. Vertical scales differ by series. These panels describe the screened production fits. Sampling diagnostics are reported in Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 4.

Supplementary Fig. 7 | Production JABBA chain trajectories. Retained draws of r, K and initial depletion ψ for each species and each of four chains. K uses the scaled internal JAGS units and should not be read directly as Mt. Retained draws per chain are SKJ 10,000, YFT 8,000, BET 10,000, ALB 12,500 and SBT 10,000. Actual chain identities are retained from the JAGS arrays. Trace overlap is interpreted alongside the rank Rhat, bulk/tail ESS19 and independent-seed checks.
Supplementary Table 5 | Verified regional assessment context
Supplementary Table 6 | Pressure-test scenario factors and simulation counts

Supplementary Fig. 8 | Future configurations and simulation stages. a, The full crossing of capacity growth, technology creep, WEO and retirement regime, with slight horizontal displacement to display coincident settings. b, Counts of fleet simulations at each stage. Analytical screens require no fleet simulations. The Shapley stage evaluates every four-measure subset; baseline configurations are reused for matched comparisons.

Supplementary Fig. 9 | Fuel properties, screening and transition depth. a, Economically adjusted lifecycle intensity in 2050 by fuel and WEO. b, Selected drop-in and newbuild adoption nodes; shares describe separate interventions. c, Screening reductions and fuel-cost effort multipliers for 14 fuel paths at three intensities per WEO. H2 denotes fossil hydrogen and H2G green hydrogen. d, Single-fuel and HVO-plus-device analytical trajectories at WEO-bound intensity, scaled by each WEO’s fixed-catch target BAU median; these are proxies, not vessel-by-vessel fuel simulations. Negative values reflect prescribed electricity credits. Panel data and fuel inputs are preserved.
Supplementary Table 7 | Fuel properties and selected transition nodes

Supplementary Fig. 10 | Consolidation schedule and accounting. a, Prescribed linear transition schedule. b, The corresponding operating-time factor 1 − 0.243 S. c, A 1,000 kW accounting example showing equal installed power in retired and replacement capacity. Panel c is illustrative and does not show an observed fleet event. Structural replacements use larger templates within organisation–gear groups; forced retirement has a separate effort-conservation rule.

Supplementary Fig. 11 | Species quota assignments and effort screening. a, Selected FMSY fractions: 100% for SKJ, YFT, BET and ALB, and 70% for SBT. b, Conditional terminal B/K with the final-year criterion at 0.25. c, Ecological effort multipliers across species and technology rates for C-type 100%-MSY and selected F-type rules. Hollow markers denote terminal B/K <0.25. The guard is an final-year selection criterion, not an annual sustainability guarantee. Results use the original conditional stock projections.

Supplementary Fig. 12 | Global sensitivity and SHAP attribution. a, Mean absolute SHAP values34 from the production random-forest surrogate fitted to 2,000 sensitivity draws. b, Draw-level contributions for the eight leading features, with colour representing the within-feature rank of its input value. These are surrogate explanations under the sampled assumptions. The additional 400-draw held-out diagnostic is reported in Supplementary Table 8.

Supplementary Fig. 13 | Historical parameter ranges and future configuration ranges. a, Annual historical Monte Carlo medians and 5th–95th percentiles across 500 draws. b, Annual baseline medians, interquartile ranges and 5th–95th percentiles across 81 specified futures. The historical band is a central 90% parameter range; the future bands describe scenario variation and are not confidence intervals. Cumulative historical bounds are calculated by summing paired draws before taking quantiles.
Supplementary Table 8 | Sensitivity selection and surrogate diagnostic
Supplementary Table 9 | Evidence types and limits of retained checks
Supplementary Table 10 | Comparison of modelled fuel consumption and GHG emissions with independent studies

Supplementary Fig. 14 | External benchmarking of fuel use and GHG emission estimates. a,b, Fishing-vessel fuel intensity for PS and LL, matched by activity year and broad geographic domain. Filled symbols show model central estimates; hollow symbols literature values. Lines connect descriptive comparisons, not uncertainty intervals. c, Model combustion-only GHG versus the ISSF 2023 diesel case. Upstream fuel supply is excluded from both plotted estimates. d, Spanish PS full-LCA context in 2003; the literature includes delivery to Galicia and shares background sources, so the systems are not matched. The 2009 PS survey family informs model operating-day assumptions; the 2023 survey supplies independent fuel outcomes. Catch species, fleet samples and attribution remain imperfectly matched. Sources and scope decisions are given in S6.4 and Supplementary Table 10.
Supplementary Table 11 | Engine-clock sensitivity at fixed fleet states

Supplementary Fig. 15 | Engine-clock sensitivity at fixed vessel states. a, Annual GHG with central 90% selected-parameter ranges from the rescaled 500 paired historical process draws. b, Cumulative 1950–2025 GHG and paired-draw 5th–95th percentiles. c, 2023 Pacific LL fuel intensity under each clock, compared with the unchanged survey value of 1,523.3 L t⁻¹. Industrial/coastal hours are scaled together for main and auxiliary engines; the small coastal gasoline model has no auxiliary engine. Fuel and the base-clock bait proxy scale with the prescribed hours; material processes and leakage stay fixed. Catch, annual days, power, allocation and fleet/stock states are unchanged. These are accounting sensitivities, not new coupled simulations or estimates of observed operating hours. The imperfect survey population and catch match remains.

Supplementary Fig. 16 | Regional and fleet-object technology-based mitigation. a, Median cumulative organisation-level reductions for individual and combined technology packages against matched fixed-catch target baselines at WEO-bound intensity. b, Object-level reductions for selected higher-emission organisation–species–gear objects. Objects meet the 60th-percentile baseline-emission screen. Colour and labels show actual reduction percentages; negative values are retained. Attribution and fleet composition contribute to the effects, which differ from global annual reductions.

Supplementary Fig. 17 | Baseline factor contrasts. The mean 2025–2050 baseline increase is contrasted with futures fixing WEO, growth, turnover or technology at the documented central setting. These one-factor reference contrasts are not Shapley contributions; a residual closes the displayed sum. Other panels show WEO endpoint distributions and analytical effort and fuel proxies. Stock-fitting and numerical-floor limitations apply.

Supplementary Fig. 18 | Whole-chain capacity and resource sensitivity. a, Original fixed-catch target emissions and feasible-catch 365-day BAU, quota, fuel and combined trajectories; ribbons span scenario percentiles 5–95. b, Paired endpoint reductions under 365- and 280-day bounds. c, Cumulative inventory-scope catch and whole-fleet GHG in 2025–2050. d, Exact Shapley contributions from all 16 rerun measure subsets in each of 81 futures. Negative effects are retained. These bounds are operational assumptions, not profitability thresholds or posterior intervals.

Supplementary Fig. 19 | Catch scale and period-intensity decomposition. a, Two-factor cumulative LMDI contributions for C- and F-type quota rules relative to each feasible-catch BAU. Box summaries are shown separately; component medians need not sum, although every paired decomposition closes. b, Cumulative catch and period CEI. c,d, Nine additional annual stock–fleet comparisons match cumulative F-type catch to a 65%-MSY C-type rule within ±1%. F fractions were tuned by repeated reruns. These tests hold the future configuration fixed but compare different quota fractions; they do not assert equal-catch benefits for the original 100%-FMSY rule.

Supplementary Fig. 20 | Regional conditional refits and historical-state feasibility checks. a, Indian Ocean BET (1975–2024) and historical YFT (1950–2020) total-biomass fits with posterior 95% ranges. b, Maximum rank Rhat and minimum bulk/tail ESS across monitored states and parameters. c, Paired GHG comparisons for 100% and 80% FMSY, fuels and combined measures in conditional regional fleet components. BET uses a 2024 reference state; YFT uses its 2020 historical state. d, Advancing historical YFT with subsequent reported catches yields negative biomass when 2024 removals are applied. Negative values diagnose model incompatibility and are never used to drive simulations. Passing MCMC convergence criteria does not establish current stock validity.
